accepted.question_text: In integer trigonometry, an angle with integer vertex has an LLS-sequence (a0, a1, a2, ...) and integer tangent Itan(BAC) = [a0; a1 : a2 : ...], while integer cosine is defined by Icos(BAC) = Isin(BAC) / Itan(BAC). Find an integer cosine rule for integer triangles stated entirely in these integer-geometric invariants.

evidence.quote: Definition 1.2. Let BAC be an angle with integer vertex and the LLS-sequence (a0, a1, a2, . . .). Then Itan(BAC) = [a0; a1 : a2 : . . .], Icos(BAC) = Isin(BAC) / Itan(BAC).
The integer sine rule for integer triangles holds in integer settings, while the integer cosine rule is unknown. Problem 1. Find an integer cosine rule for integer triangles in integer trigonometry.

accepted.question_text: For integer polygons, each angle has an LLS-sequence, and the LLS-sequence is the complete invariant of an integer angle in this setting. Classify all n-tuples of LLS-sequences that can occur as the angle data of integer n-gons.

evidence.quote: LLS-sequence is the complete invariant of integer angles in integer geometry.
Problem 2. (IKEA problem.) Classify all n-tuples of LLS-sequences for the angles that form integer n-gons.

accepted.question_text: A sail is the boundary of C \ LS, where C is a cone of a hyperplane arrangement and LS is the union of all subsets U similar to a chosen model subset S that avoid a chosen subset L. Classify all combinatorially possible types of faces that can occur on such sails, especially for Klein polyhedra where S is a basis n-simplex and L = Z^n intersected with the punctured cone C.

evidence.quote: Definition 2.2. Let C be a cone of some arrangement, and let S be one of its subsets. For an arbitrary subset L ∈ C we define the set LS = ⋃_{U∩L=∅, U∼S} U. The boundary of C \ LS is called the sail of L ⊂ C with respect to S.
Problem 3. Classify all combinatorial possible types of faces. This question targets mostly Klein polyhedra (i.e., Sail△n,Zn∩C˙(C)).

accepted.question_text: An n-dimensional simplex is called empty when its intersection with the integer lattice Z^n consists exactly of its vertices. Classify all empty simplices of dimension n up to affine integer-lattice congruence.

evidence.quote: A polyhedron P is said to be empty if its intersection with Z^n is precisely the set of vertices of P. We have the following problem. Problem 4. Classify all empty simplices of dimension n up to lattice congruence.

accepted.question_text: For an m-dimensional continued fraction in the geometric sense of the paper, determine which integer n-gons can occur as faces. This includes both faces at integer distance 1 from the origin and faces at integer distance greater than 1 from the origin.

evidence.quote: Problem 5. Which n-gons are realizable as faces of an m-dimensional continued fraction?
Here are two essentially geometrically different subcases: • Faces at integer distance 1 to the origin ... • Faces at integer distance greater than 1 to the origin ...

accepted.question_text: Suppose k runners start together on a circular track of circumference 1 and run with distinct constant speeds. Is it true that, for every chosen runner, there exists a time when that runner is lonely, meaning at arc distance at least 1/k from every other runner?

evidence.quote: Problem 6. ( Lonely Runner conjecture.) Assume that k runners start a competition at the a common point of the circular track with circumference 1. Let them all have distinct constant speeds. Then for any given runner, there is a time at which that runner is lonely, i.e., at arc distance at least 1/k away from every other runners.

accepted.question_text: Describe all finite two-dimensional sails, and thereby all corresponding continued fractions, in the geometric multidimensional-continued-fraction setting.

evidence.quote: Problem 7. Describe all finite two-dimensional sails (and the corresponding continued fractions).

accepted.question_text: For polytopes of a fixed combinatorial type, describe the collections of sails of the associated cones arising from all such polytopes.

evidence.quote: Problem 8. (Multidimensional IKEA problem.) Describe the collections of the sails of the cones for all polytopes of a given combinatorial type.

accepted.question_text: Does there exist an algorithm that decides whether a specified combinatorial type of fundamental domain can be realized by a periodic continued fraction?

evidence.quote: Problem 9. (V. Arnold.) Does there exist an algorithm to decide whether a given type of fundamental domain is realizable by a periodic continued fraction?

accepted.question_text: If two Klein sails are not integer congruent, must their torus decompositions be different? Here a torus decomposition means the collection of integer-congruence types of the polyhedra in a fundamental domain together with their integer distances to the vertex of the cone.

evidence.quote: A torus decomposition corresponding to a periodic sail in the sense of Klein is the collections of integer congruence types of polyhedra in any fundamental domain endowed with the integer distances to the vertex of the cone.
Conjecture 10. (V. Arnold.) Torus decompositions of integer noncongruent Klein sails are distinct.

accepted.question_text: Describe all torus decompositions that are realized by periodic two-dimensional continued fractions, where the torus decomposition records the integer-congruence types of polyhedra in a fundamental domain together with their integer distances to the cone vertex.

evidence.quote: A torus decomposition corresponding to a periodic sail in the sense of Klein is the collections of integer congruence types of polyhedra in any fundamental domain endowed with the integer distances to the vertex of the cone.
Problem 11. (V. Arnold.) Describe all torus decompositions that are realized by periodic two-dimensional continued fractions.

accepted.question_text: Must the torus decomposition of every algebraic sail in the sense of Klein contain at least one face that is integer congruent to a triangle, at least one face at integer distance 1 from the cone vertex, and at least one face at integer distance greater than 1 from the cone vertex?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 12. The torus decomposition of every algebraic sail in the sense of Klein contains at least one face that is • integer congruent to a triangle; • at the unit integer distance form the vertex of the cone; • at the integer distance from the vertex of the cone greater than 1.

accepted.question_text: Classify the continued fractions that correspond to the same cubic extension of the field of rational numbers Q.

evidence.quote: Problem 13. (V. Arnold.) Classify continued fractions that correspond to the same cubic extension of the field of rational numbers.

accepted.question_text: For dimensions n >= 3, prove the existence of a cone whose sail realizes a single prescribed non-periodic combinatorial structure.

evidence.quote: Problem 14. Prove the existence of a cone for a single non-periodic combinatorial structure (n ≥ 3).

accepted.question_text: For n-dimensional continued fractions in dimensions n >= 3, determine which faces have the highest relative frequencies.

evidence.quote: Here we would like to outline the following three questions (which are open for n ≥ 3). Problem 15. Find frequencies on n-dimensional continued fractions with the highest relative frequencies.

accepted.question_text: For every positive integer constant C, are there only finitely many pairwise integer non-congruent faces whose relative frequencies exceed C?

evidence.quote: Problem 16. For every positive integer constant C there exist only finitely many pairwise integer non-congruent faces with frequencies exceeding C.

accepted.question_text: In dimensions n >= 3, is the sum of the relative frequencies of all possible faces finite?

evidence.quote: Problem 17. Is that true that sum of all relative frequencies for all possible faces is finite for higher dimensions (n ≥ 3)?

accepted.question_text: If the sum of the relative frequencies of all possible faces is finite in dimensions n >= 3, find the correct higher-dimensional analogue of the Gauss map and compare its face frequencies with the frequencies defined by Möbius geometry.

evidence.quote: Problem 18. In case of positive answer to the above question find the generalization of the Gauss map and compare the corresponding frequencies of faces with the related frequencies coming from Möbius geometry.

accepted.question_text: Find a natural generalization of the Farey tessellation to higher-dimensional hyperbolic geometry.

evidence.quote: Problem 19. Find a natural generalization of the Farey tessellation to higher-dimensional hyperbolic geometry.

accepted.question_text: Let K be a totally real cubic number field, and let y and z be elements of K with 0 < y, z < 1 such that 1, y, and z are linearly independent over Q. Does the Jacobi-Perron algorithm started from v = (1, y, z) always produce an eventually periodic continued fraction?

evidence.quote: Problem 20. (Jacobi’s last theorem.) Let K be a totally real cubic number field. Consider arbitrary elements y and z of K such that 0 < y, z < 1 (here we assume that 1, y, and z are independent over Q). Is it true that the Jacobi-Perron algorithm generates an eventually periodic continued fraction with starting data v = (1, y, z).

accepted.question_text: Study the geometric properties of the Markov spectrum.

evidence.quote: Problem 21. Study geometric properties of Markov spectrum.

accepted.question_text: Generalize continued fractions so that they describe 3-bridge knots, in analogy with the way ordinary finite continued fractions give a complete invariant of rational knots, also called two-bridge knots.

evidence.quote: Recall that ordinary finite continued fractions provide a complete invariant to rational knots, known also as two-bridge knots. So the following rather classical question is actual. Problem 22. Generalize continued fractions to describe 3-bridge knots.

needs_review.question_text_raw: For the case of Klein sails it is still unknown if there exists a two-dimensional periodic sail which contains only quadrangles, even a single quadrangle in the fundamental domain.

evidence.quote: Remark. For the case of Klein sails (i.e., Sail△,Zn∩C˙(C).) it is still unknown if there exists a two-dimensional periodic sail which contains only quadrangles (even a single quadrangle in the fundamental domain).

needs_review.question_text_raw: Find an adequate complete invariant of polyhedra that appear as faces at sails.

evidence.quote: • Find an adequate complete invariant of polyhedra that appear as faces at sails.

needs_review.question_text_raw: Find an adequate complete invariant of cones up to integer congruences.

evidence.quote: • Find an adequate complete invariant of cones up to integer congruences.

needs_review.question_text_raw: Study the face distribution of sails (generalized Gauss-Kuzmin distribution).

evidence.quote: • Study the face distribution of sails (generalized Gauss-Kuzmin distribution).
